activity: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
knowledge_domain: babysitting a neighbor's child for the first time
fact: A young child can drown in just a few inches of water and without splashing or crying out, so children should never be left alone in or near a bath.
story:
Stella had read the note on the fridge three times before Mrs. Hale left: Charlie, age two, dinner at six, bath at six thirty, no snacks after five. Now the clock said six twenty-eight, and Charlie was standing in the tub patting the shallow water like it was a drum. Two inches of water, Stella figured, maybe three. She knelt beside the tub with the yellow rubber duck and tried to sound like someone who had done this a hundred times.

The phone rang in the kitchen. Stella's stomach tightened, because Mrs. Hale had written "call if anything comes up," and the ring seemed to fill the whole house. Charlie laughed and poured a cup of water over his own head, splashing droplets onto her sleeve.

"Stay right there, buddy," she started to say, and then she stopped. She remembered the safety workshop from last summer, the lifeguard with the whistle, and one sentence that had stuck to her like a burr: a young child can drown in just a few inches of water, and without splashing or crying out, so children should never be left alone in or near a bath. It had sounded impossible then. Two inches of water, and no noise at all? But the lifeguard had been completely impartial about it, no drama, just the facts, and that was somehow worse.

So Stella pulled the big frog towel off the hook, lifted Charlie out of the tub, dripping and squealing, and wrapped him up like a burrito. She carried him down the hall with water soaking through her shirt, the phone still ringing. "Coming, coming," she muttered, shifting Charlie to her hip to grab the receiver.

It was Mrs. Hale, calling to say she'd be home by seven fifteen instead of seven, and traffic was terrible, and was everything all right? Stella said Charlie was clean, fed, and wearing a towel, and she heard Mrs. Hale laugh for the first time all evening. When she hung up, Charlie patted her cheek with a wet hand.

Back in the bathroom, Stella dried him and dressed him in dinosaur pajamas while he tried to steal the rubber duck's hat, which did not exist, which was the whole joke as far as Charlie was concerned. She let him win the argument. Her science teacher would have called her a decomposer of fun, she thought, breaking down perfectly good games into rules, but tonight the rules had felt like the right kind.

At seven fifteen the door opened, and Mrs. Hale stood there with rain on her coat. Charlie barreled into her legs shouting "baff, baff," and Stella stood behind him holding the wet frog towel. "He had a great bath," she said. "He was with me the whole time." Mrs. Hale looked at her for a second, then smiled and said the words every first-time babysitter wants to hear: "Same time Thursday?"

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: Squash plants grow separate male and female flowers, and only a female flower, which has a tiny fruit at its base, can grow into a squash after being pollinated.
story:
Ivy pressed her nose against the fencing of the demo garden at Martelli's Garden Center, where her mother shopped every Saturday for bags of soil and trays of tomato seedlings. Behind the fence grew a squash plant the size of a small tent, its leaves broad as dinner plates and its yellow flowers glowing like tiny lanterns in the morning light. Ivy had counted twenty-one blossoms on it last week, and today she counted again.

"Twenty-six," she reported to Priya, who worked the register and let Ivy hang around as long as she didn't trample anything. "Twenty-six flowers. That's a record."

"Beautiful, right?" Priya said. "That plant's been blooming for a month."

Then Ivy saw something that ruined her whole morning. Beneath the biggest blossom, tucked against the stem, hung a single squash the size of her thumb. One. She searched the entire plant, parting leaves, checking every branch. One squash, twenty-six flowers. "Priya, why is there only one? Something's wrong with it."

Priya came over, wiped her hands on her apron, and peered at the plant with her. "Mr. Martelli says that happens sometimes. He shrugs and says the plant's moody." She lowered her voice. "I think he just doesn't know."

That wasn't good enough for Ivy. She took out the little notebook she carried for garden observations, because she had a concept she was testing: if a plant makes flowers, flowers should make fruit, and if they don't, something hidden must be blocking the way. On Sunday she went back with her mother and stood at the fence for an hour, staring. Slowly she noticed that the blossoms weren't all the same. Most of them sat flat on the stem, thin at the bottom, and when they closed and faded, they dropped off and left nothing behind. A few were different. Underneath them, at the base, swelled a tiny green bump, a miniature squash no bigger than a pencil eraser.

She checked every one. The plain flowers: no bump, no squash ever. The bumped ones: a squash started. And there were only two bumped ones on the whole enormous plant, and one of those had shriveled and turned brown, its little squash shriveling with it. She wrote it all down. The bump flowers were the only ones that could become squash, and even they weren't guaranteed.

She asked Priya to borrow the store's gardening book, and they sat on stacked bags of mulch turning pages until Ivy found a chapter with diagrams. There it was. "They're female," she said, jabbing the page. "The ones with the little fruit at the base. The plain ones are male. Both kinds of flowers grow on the same plant, but only the females can turn into squash." She read on, lips moving. "And the female has to be pollinated, pollen has to reach it, or the little fruit just dies."

"Which explains why Mr. Martelli's plant is moody," Priya said. "Twenty-four males and two females. Terrible odds."

Ivy refused to comply with those odds. The next morning, before the flowers closed in the heat, she came back with a soft paintbrush from her art kit. She found a freshly opened male flower, brushed its center gently, and carried the dust of pollen on the bristles to the one remaining female, with its swelling base, and touched the brush to her stigma, careful as putting on a Band-Aid. She tied a strip of blue yarn below the blossom so she could find it again.

A week later she knelt at the fence, following the blue yarn with her eyes. The flower had faded and fallen, but the little fruit beneath it had grown fat and firm, as long as her hand now, striped green and pale. "Priya!" she called across the lot. "Come see!"

Priya jogged over, looked, and let out a whoop. Then she pointed at the fence gate. "Go tell Martelli. He's been blaming the weather for years."

activity: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
knowledge_domain: attending a religious or cultural celebration with family
fact: A Hanukkah menorah, or hanukkiah, has nine branches: eight for the eight nights of the holiday and one for the shamash, the helper candle used to light the others.
story:
Autumn pushed through the festival crowd with her cousin Jaylen and their new neighbor, Priya, who had moved to town just last week. The street was lined with booths of latkes, jelly donuts, and crafts, and at the far end, on a long table, someone had set up a huge silver menorah. Priya stopped and stared at it.

"Wait," Priya said, counting the branches with her finger. "Eight nights of Hanukkah, but that thing has nine candles. Somebody messed up?"

Autumn looked at the menorah, then at Priya, then back at the menorah. She had lit one at her grandmother's house every year, but she had never really counted. One, two, three. Priya was right. Nine. Her first thought was that the festival committee had made a mistake, but her grandmother had a menorah at home too, and Autumn was suddenly sure it also had nine. She grabbed Jaylen's sleeve. "Come with me. I need to check something."

They wove back through the crowd to her grandmother's booth, where Bubbe was selling knitted scarves to raise money to donate to the food pantry. "Bubbe," Autumn asked, "your menorah at home has nine candles too, right? Not eight?"

Bubbe laughed. "Look at the ones on the shelf, sweetheart." The small menorahs for sale each held nine candles, and in every one of them, one candle sat higher or off to the side, apart from the row of eight. Autumn picked one up and turned it over in her hands. The odd candle out was set apart on purpose. Someone nearby was explaining to a visitor, and the visitor nodded and repeated the word to her friend: "The ninth one is called the shamash." Autumn held the little menorah up so Priya could see the taller branch.

"So the ninth one isn't a mistake," Priya said slowly. "It's for lighting the others." Autumn grinned. "Eight for the eight nights, plus one helper." She set the menorah down and pointed across the street, where a man was getting ready to light the giant silver one at dusk. "Come on, let's watch. You'll see which candle does the work."

They found a spot near the front just as the man lifted the shamash from its high branch, touched it to the first candle, and returned it to its place above the others. The flame held steady against the darkening sky, and the crowd around them cheered. Priya counted the unlit candles left on the row. "Seven to go," she said. "I'll be here every night." Autumn bumped her shoulder against Priya's. "Save us a spot," she said.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Swallowing or yawning opens the Eustachian tubes, which lets air into the middle ear and relieves the pressure people feel in their ears as a plane descends.
story:
Alexia sat on a flat rock at the edge of the campsite, turning the safety card from the airplane over in her hands. Around her the pines stood in rows, and somewhere behind the tents a woodpecker knocked at a dead trunk. The card, which she had tucked into her backpack without thinking, portrayed a little cartoon passenger chewing something, and that picture had been bothering her since the flight two days ago.

She let herself go back to it. The plane had been dropping through clouds toward the airport, and her little brother Theo had started crying, pressing his hands over his ears and saying they hurt, they hurt. Their mom had dug through the seat pocket, found a juice box, and handed it to him. He had swallowed three times, and then, like a switch flipping, he had stopped. Alexia had felt her own ears plug up during that same descent, a tight stuffed feeling, and she had yawned because she was tired. After the yawn, her ears had cleared with a soft pop. At the time she thought it was luck. Now, on the rock, she lined the moments up side by side: swallowing, yawning, relief.

"So the chewing on the card isn't about being hungry," she said to Theo, who was poking a beetle with a stick. Theo was six and generally eccentric in his habits, wearing his sweatshirt backward and refusing sandwiches cut into triangles, but he looked up anyway.

"We're driving down the pass tomorrow," Alexia said. "It goes down a long way, and last time my ears did the same thing they did on the plane. I think swallowing or yawning is the factor that fixes it. It opens what the card called the Eustachian tubes, and air gets into your middle ear and the pressure lets go." Theo squinted at her. "You can test it with me," she said. "If I'm wrong, we'll both be grumpy, and if I'm right, we won't."

The next morning the car wound down the pass, and the pressure built just as she remembered, like someone pushing on her eardrums with both thumbs. "Now," she said, and she swallowed, hard, twice. Pop. The full feeling drained away, and the hiss of the tires came back sharp and clear. Theo made an enormous theatrical yawn, jaw stretched wide, and then blinked. "My ears went boom," he reported, "but the good boom."

From the front seat their dad glanced in the mirror and smiled but said nothing, which Alexia appreciated. She watched the valley open below them, the river showing silver where the sun caught it, and she thought about the card in her backpack, the little cartoon passenger chewing away. At the bottom of the pass Theo held up his water bottle, took a long swallow, and announced to the whole car, "My ears feel like butterflies now."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Caramelization is browning that happens when sugar alone is heated, which makes it a different reaction from the Maillard reaction, which also needs amino acids.
story:
Layla set the pot of sugar and water on the burner and turned the dial to medium. Her grandmother's caramel recipe had one line of instruction, "Cook until amber," which Layla felt implied a confidence she did not share. Behind her, her cousin Marcus leaned against the counter of the school cooking classroom, watching the pot like it might attack him.

"Is this the same browning as the crust on the roast at Sunday dinner?" he asked. "Because that smells way better than this."

Layla thought about it while stirring. The roast crust had come from meat, and meat was full of protein. The pot in front of her held nothing but sugar and water. If the browning were one single thing, then sugar alone should not be able to do it, since the roast clearly needed something the sugar did not have. She turned the burner up a notch, and the thermostat clicked somewhere inside the stove.

"It can't be the same," she said. "This is just sugar and water. There's nothing else in here."

"So?"

"So the roast has protein in it, and this doesn't. Two different things can't need the exact same stuff to brown." She kept watching, and the pale liquid began to turn gold at the edges, then deeper, without a single speck of anything else in the pot. Sugar alone, browning anyway.

Marcus squinted at it. "Then what do you call this one?"

"Caramelization," Layla said. "The roast one is the Maillard reaction, and that one also needs amino acids." She had read the two terms on a card in her science folder last week, and now, watching sugar turn amber all by itself, the card finally made sense.

The smell hit them both at once, buttery and dark, and Marcus made a sound like a deflating balloon. "That smells amazing. In vain did I resist it," he announced, reaching for a spoon.

"That's not how you use that word."

"Fine. I resisted it, and I failed." He dipped the spoon in anyway, and the caramel stretched off it in a long thread that landed on his sleeve. He shrieked and danced backward into the cart of mixing bowls, which rattled like a passing train.

Layla grabbed the pot off the heat, poured the caramel into a bowl, and handed Marcus the spoon. "You earned that one," she said. "Now hold still while I take the picture for Grandma."

activity: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
knowledge_domain: hosting a grandparent who comes to stay for a week
fact: A pill organizer has a compartment for each day of the week, so an empty compartment shows that day's dose has already been taken.
story:
Grandpa Ray arrived on Sunday with one suitcase, one crossword book, and a plastic box with seven little lids, each printed with a day of the week. Cameron's mom put the box on the kitchen counter and said, "Grandpa, your pills are in there, sorted by day. That's the whole system." Grandpa Ray tapped the lids twice, like he was checking that they were real.

The trouble started Monday morning. Cameron was eating toast in the backyard, watching Grandpa Ray water the tomato plants in the arid corner of the garden where nothing ever grew, when Grandpa suddenly stopped. "Did I take my pills this morning?" he asked the tomatoes. Then he asked Cameron. Cameron hadn't seen him take anything, and Grandpa couldn't remember walking back inside, which was annoying, because if he skipped the pills he felt dizzy later, and if he took them twice, Cameron's mom had said, they had to call the doctor.

Grandpa started toward the house to take them just in case. Cameron jumped up from the picnic table. "Wait. Don't take any yet." He was thinking about the box, the way a detective thinks about footprints. If Grandpa had already taken his morning pills, then one lid would be open and one compartment would be empty. If he hadn't, the compartment would still be full. You couldn't see the past, but the box could show it anyway. Cameron ran inside, slid down on his knees at the counter, and flipped open the lid marked Monday. Empty. "You took them, Grandpa. Monday's compartment is empty."

Grandpa Ray squinted at the box, then at Cameron, then grinned. "You solved it before I even broke anything. Remind me to put you in my will." Cameron felt a little swell of pride, which lasted until Tuesday morning, when the same thing happened again, and again on Wednesday. By Thursday, Cameron's pride had started to radiate less warmth and more resentment. He was spending his whole week being a pill butler while his friends were at the pool.

Then came the twist. On Saturday, Cameron opened the Saturday compartment and found it empty, but Saturday's pills were supposed to be filled next. His stomach dropped. Grandpa hadn't taken Saturday's dose. Cameron checked the other compartments and found them all empty too, and then he remembered: Wednesday afternoon, Grandpa had stood at the counter, shaking the box, saying he was "reorganizing for efficiency." He had dumped the pills into his hand, sorted them by color, and put them back wherever he liked.

"Grandpa," Cameron said, holding up the box, "the compartments don't mean anything anymore. You alphabetized your pills."

"I sorted them by color, actually," said Grandpa Ray, watering the tomatoes again. "Reds on the left. Very tidy."

Cameron called his mom at work, and she came home with a new box and a lock for the lid. Grandpa Ray held up the locked box, turned it over, and said, "Well. I suppose I've been outsmarted by a fourth-grader's invention and an eleven-year-old. My week is complete."

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Water should never be poured on a grease fire, because it turns to steam instantly and spreads the burning oil; turning off the heat and covering the pan with a lid smothers it.
story:
The community kitchen on Maple Street smelled like onions and cinnamon on Saturdays, and Dominic liked it better than any place he knew. His mother worked the lunch shift there, and today he had claimed a burner so he could fry chicken for his little sister, Ana, who had asked for it three nights in a row. He set the pan on the stove, poured in oil, and waited, watching the oil shiver and go loose as it heated.

He was cutting lemons when he heard a soft whump behind him. Flames stood up out of the pan, orange and calm, the way a candle is calm, which somehow made them worse. His hand shot toward the faucet, because water was what you threw on fire, everyone knew that. Then he stopped. Last month he had stood beside Mr. Ruiz, the kitchen's head cook, when a pan of oil flared just like this one, and Mr. Ruiz had not touched the sink. He had turned off the burner and slid a lid over the flames, flat and quick, like sliding a card across a table. The fire had gone out under it. A volunteer had grabbed a pitcher of water and Mr. Ruiz had said, "Never pour water on a grease fire," and moved the pitcher away, and that was all he had said.

Dominic reached over and shut off the burner. The flames kept dancing, so that was not enough by itself. He picked up the lid, held it sideways like Mr. Ruiz had, and slid it over the pan. The fire smothered underneath, and the kitchen went quiet except for Ana, who had wandered over and stood frozen with her lemonade.

"You put a lid on it," she said. Not a question, just amazement.

"It works because the fire can't get out," Dominic said. "Water would've made it jump everywhere." He lifted the lid a crack, saw only dark oil, and set it down again until the pan cooled. His mother hurried over from the lunch line, wiping her hands on her apron, and Ana told her the whole thing twice, the flames bigger each time.

Word traveled around the room the way good news does, and soon the volunteers began telling each other to keep a lid by every fry station. Mrs. Okafor, who ran the kitchen, gave his shoulder a squeeze. "You were quick," she said. "That kind of compassion for everybody standing near that stove is contagious, you know."

Dominic dumped the burnt oil, wiped the pan, and started over with fresh oil and the lid sitting right beside the burner, where he could reach it in one second. Ana pulled a stool up next to him.

"Teach me the lid trick," she said.

activity: making an art or craft project
knowledge_domain: making an art or craft project
fact: Clay pieces must be completely dry before they are fired in a kiln, because leftover water turns to steam and can crack or burst the piece.
story:
Joseph pressed his thumb into the rim of his clay bowl one more time, trying to decide whether to modify the wavy edge or leave it alone. The bowl was his best work all summer, and tomorrow was the firing day at the community art studio.

"That one's coming with us," said Marisol, the student helper, stacking pieces on the cart by the kiln. She lifted a small bowl made by a kid named Theo, then set it back down on the shelf instead. "Sorry, Theo. Yours stays out this round."

Theo's shoulders dropped. "Why? Mine's just as good as his."

"I can't put yours in," Marisol said, and moved on to the next cart.

Joseph watched Theo stare at his bowl, chin wobbling. He knew that look. Last year Joseph had cried in this same room when his coil pot came out of the kiln cracked down the middle, and nobody could tell him why.

He walked over and picked up Theo's bowl. His own bowl, waiting on the cart, had felt light and chalky all the way through when he'd tapped it that morning. Theo's bowl was light at the rim, too. But when Joseph turned it over and pressed his palm flat against the thick bottom, the clay felt cool, almost like a cellar floor. His own bowl's bottom had felt like dry sidewalk.

He carried both bowls to the window and held them side by side in the bright light, using the glare almost like a lens to hunt for differences. Theo's bowl had a dull, darker patch across the base, a shadow of color where his own bowl was evenly pale. Something was still hiding in that clay, something he couldn't see directly but could find by touch and by looking.

"Hey, Theo," Joseph said. "Your bowl isn't the problem. The bottom's still damp. Mine was like that last year, and it cracked in the kiln. Water left in clay turns to steam, and steam can crack or even burst the whole piece."

Theo peered at the dark patch. "So it's not ruined?"

"It just has to dry all the way through first. Leave it on the sunny shelf by the window till next week." Joseph set it there himself, turning the damp side toward the sun. Then he went back for a scrap of paper and wrote FIRING NEXT WEEK, THEO'S BOWL, and propped it against the rim, where nobody could miss it.

"It'll be in the next kiln load," he said. "Promise."

Theo smiled and steadied the sign with one careful finger.

activity: cooking or baking a meal for the family
knowledge_domain: cooking or baking a meal for the family
fact: Yeast makes bread rise by feeding on sugars and releasing carbon dioxide gas, which gets trapped in the dough as bubbles.
story:
Jordan set up his table between the honey seller and the apple farmer, his mother's folding griddle stacked with mixing bowls, bags of flour, and a jar of yeast he'd carried carefully from home. His plan was simple: bake flatbreads and one real loaf for his family's booth at the market, because tonight was his turn to cook and he wanted it to be bread, real risen bread, the kind his grandmother made. He had promised his little sister a slice still warm enough to melt butter.

He measured the flour, stirred in a spoonful of sugar, and mixed the yeast with water from the market's hot kettle, thinking warm water would wake the yeast up faster. The dough came together smooth and springy, and he draped a cloth over the bowl the way his grandmother did. But half an hour later, when he peeked, the dough sat flat and heavy as a hull of concrete. He waited another half hour. Nothing.

"Your dough's not doing anything," said Marisol from the next booth, leaning over with a crate of plums. "Mine always puffs up when my mom makes it."

"Yeast makes bread rise," Jordan said slowly, mostly to himself. "It feeds on the sugars in the dough, and the gas it gives off, carbon dioxide, gets trapped in little bubbles. That's what pushes it up." He looked at the bowl, then at the kettle still steaming behind the counter. Something was wrong with the yeast itself, something he couldn't see. He tested the only idea he had. He ran fresh water, let it cool until it felt only faintly warm on his wrist, like testing a bottle for a baby, and started a new batch with a fresh spoonful of yeast.

While the second bowl rested under its cloth, he watched the kettle. The first water had been hot enough to sting his fingers when he rinsed them. He cupped a little of the new water in his palm and held it for a full minute. No sting.

"Jordan, look," Marisol whispered, poking his arm. He lifted the cloth. The dough had climbed over the rim of the bowl, rounded and swollen, and when he pressed one finger into it, the dent filled slowly back in. His grin must have been contagious, because Marisol laughed and the honey seller gave him a thumbs-up. He punched the dough down, shaped it into a loaf, and slid it onto the griddle. His sister ran up just as the smell reached the end of the aisle. "Is it ready?" she asked. He wrapped the first slice in a napkin and handed it over, steam curling into the morning air.

activity: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
knowledge_domain: the way averages, percentages and rankings in sports and news compress many events into one number
fact: The NFL's passer rating combines several passing statistics into one number on a scale from 0 to a maximum of 158.3.
story:
The meatloaf was half gone when Marcus climbed onto his chair and pointed at the phone propped against the salt shaker. "Dad, it says this quarterback has a perfect rating. But it's one hundred fifty-eight point three. Why isn't perfect one hundred?"

"Finish your green beans first," Dad said, but his eyes stayed on the phone, where the game was muted and a fantasy league deadline glowed in the corner: lineup locked at 8 p.m. It was 7:41.

Gabriella reached over and slid the phone toward herself. Last summer, at the lake, Uncle Ray had leaned back in a folding chair and read numbers off the radio like they were a weather report: completion percentage, yards, touchdowns, interceptions. She had thought it was strange even then, that one number could stand in for all of those. "I think I know," she said. "Remember Uncle Ray? He said one number smushed everything together." She scrolled, and there it was on the stats page, rows of passing numbers stacked under a single figure at the top. "See, they take a bunch of passing stats and combine them into one number. That's why it's weird. It's not out of a hundred because it isn't counting one thing."

Marcus squinted at the screen. "One hundred fifty-eight point three out of what?"

"Out of zero up to the maximum," Gabriella said. "Zero is the worst, one hundred fifty-eight point three is the best there is. It's called a passer rating."

Dad set down his fork. "So a perfect game isn't a hundred, it's one fifty-eight three."

"Right. Zero to one fifty-eight point three." She tapped the little bar graph beside it. Each passing stat was a separate component, and the app showed them stacked like layers before they got squashed into that single score at the top.

Marcus picked up a green bean and studied it like it was the last puzzle piece. "So one number is like, lots of games all pressed into one?"

"Lots of throws, lots of games, everything," Gabriella said. She remembered her class project in the fall, when she had averaged her five math quizzes and the average made one bad test look not so bad and one great one look smaller than it felt. Numbers did that. They took a whole messy season and pressed it flat, like flowers in a book.

Dad glanced at the clock. 7:52. His fantasy decision was due in eight minutes, and his old quarterback had a rating of 71.2 while the new one sat at 104.8. "Help me," he said. "Is higher better?"

"Higher is better," Gabriella said, "as long as it's the same kind of number." She pulled the phone closer and started comparing the rows underneath, the completions and yards that the ratings had compressed. Marcus leaned against her arm, breathing meatloaf breath, and slid his empty bean plate to the far side of his tray like a prisoner hiding evidence.

At 7:58, Dad tapped start on the new quarterback. The screen flashed green, then the kitchen light refracted off the phone's glass and threw a small wobbling rainbow across the tablecloth. Marcus laughed his infectious, squeaking laugh and chased the rainbow with his fork, and Dad stood up to get the ice cream, which was his way of saying thank you without saying it.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Hypotheses are often written as 'If ..., then ...' statements, which name the change being made and the result that is predicted.
story:
Hannah stared at the lopsided bean plants along the back fence and knew her science fair poster was doomed. It said, in fat green letters, Plants Like Music, and her teacher had written one question in the margin: How could that be tested? The beans had grown next to the speaker she dragged outside every afternoon, but her brother Theo had watered them whenever he felt like it, so maybe they liked the water, not the music. Nobody at the fair would believe a poster built on a guess she could not check.

"We can fix it," Theo said, plopping down beside her on the back steps with a peanut butter sandwich. "Mom says I have to collaborate with you anyway, since I did the watering."

"You collaborated too much," Hannah said. "That's the problem." She pulled her notebook out of her back pocket and flipped to a page with the word HYPOTHESIS circled twice. She had found it in her science book the night before. "It says here hypotheses are often written as 'If, then' statements. Like, if I make a change, then I predict a result. The change and the prediction both go right in the sentence."

"So write one."

"Fine. If I play music to one tray of beans and no music to another, then the music tray will grow taller." She said it out loud twice, and it sounded like a real experiment instead of a poster with a blob of glue on it. "But both trays get the same water, same spot, same everything else. Only one thing changes."

They set up two trays of new seeds on the picnic table, counted out twenty seeds apiece, and marked the music tray with a strip of tape. Their father's toy sailboat sat at the end of the table, waiting for its broken rudder to be glued, and Hannah moved it out of the way so the shadow would not fall on either tray. "Sorry," she told the boat. "You're extinct until Saturday." Then she plugged in the speaker, faced it at tray one, and pressed play.

Every afternoon after school they measured. Theo held the ruler while Hannah wrote the numbers, and they argued about half millimeters until their mother called them in for dinner. By Friday the no-music tray was winning by three centimeters, and Hannah felt her cheeks go hot even though nobody was watching. She had predicted the wrong result.

"Poster's ruined," Theo said.

"No, it's better." Hannah turned the notebook around so he could see the graph she had started. "The test overturned my hypothesis, which means it was a real test. I'll write what actually happened." She picked up the green marker, crossed out Plants Like Music, and wrote underneath: If no music, then taller beans. "Guess the plants like quiet," she said, and pinned the page to the fence beside the trays.

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: During China's Qingming Festival, usually on April 4 or 5, families visit their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings.
story:
Alexis had never swept a gravestone before, and she was surprised at how carefully she did it, as though the granite might notice sloppy work. It was the fourth of April, the first spring since Grandpa died, and her mother had flown them to China to be with the cousins for the day. "What's today called again?" Alexis asked, working the broom into the carved grooves of his name.

"Qingming," her cousin Mei said, kneeling in the grass with a damp cloth. "It falls on April fourth or fifth. Families come to their ancestors' graves to clean them and leave offerings." She set out a bowl of rice, a few oranges, and a paper lantern folded into the shape of a bird.

Alexis looked at the offerings, then at the clean stone, then at the rows of other families along the hillside, every one of them sweeping or wiping or setting down food. A question tugged at her. Grandpa couldn't eat the rice. He couldn't see the swept stone. So what was all this for? She tested her first idea out loud. "Is it for him, or for us?"

Mei tilted her head, considering. "Maybe both."

"That's a paradox," Alexis said slowly, turning the word over. The rice was for him and not for him. She decided to run a second test. She took the last orange from the bag and placed it at the base of the stone, but then she spoke to it. "You always stole my orange slices at lunch, Grandpa. You said I had to earn them back in a staring contest." Around her the hill smelled of rain that had come overnight and would come again; the ground was saturated, dark and soft, and her sneakers sank a little with each step. Mei laughed and told a story about Grandpa hiding plum candy in his coat sleeve, a chronic habit, so reliable that the cousins used to check his pockets first thing at every visit.

The sky was turning gray, and their mothers called from down the hill that the storm would arrive within the hour, so they had to finish before the paper lantern soaked through. Mei and Alexis brushed the last leaves from the base of the stone together, and Alexis pressed her palm flat against the cool granite, once, the way she used to press her hand into Grandpa's before a staring contest.

"Why do you think the bird flies?" Alexis asked, watching the lantern bob in the rising wind.

Mei folded a small crease in its wing. "Maybe it's looking for someone to deliver the oranges to."

"Then it better hurry," Alexis said, and lifted it up into the first fat drops of rain.

activity: going to a first school dance
knowledge_domain: going to a first school dance
fact: A mirror ball turns one spotlight into hundreds of moving spots of light because each small mirror tile reflects the beam in a slightly different direction.
story:
Brody stood at the edge of the gym with his phone out, typing into the family group chat while the DJ played a song nobody danced to yet.

"Nobody's dancing," he sent. "I'm basically a coat rack with shoes."

His sister replied first, as always. "Then be the first coat rack to dance."

His mom sent a thumbs-up, which helped exactly zero percent. His grandpa typed slowly, in fragments, so Brody knew a message about "back in my day" was coming, and he would get it in about ten minutes, sentence by sentence.

He remembered the chat from last week, when the permission slip had come home. His mom had written, "He says he's not going," and his sister had answered, "He said that about the bake sale too, and then he ran the cash box." That had actually been the best part. He liked handling the commerce part, counting change, making sure the fundraiser earned what it should. His grandpa had replied, "The boy understands commerce. He'll be fine." Brody had gone to his room and smiled at that, though he'd never admit it.

Now the gym lights dimmed, and a single spotlight clicked on, aimed at the mirror ball hanging from the ceiling. Brody watched the beam hit it, and suddenly hundreds of small spots of light began to sweep across the floor, the walls, the bleachers, sliding over everybody's faces. It was like the whole room had started to glitter. Some kids stopped pretending not to care and just looked up.

A girl near the wall was watching the spots too. She wasn't dancing either. She pointed at one spot on the floor and followed it with her finger until it vanished, then found a new one. "Okay, wait," she said to nobody, then seemed to decide that Brody counted as nobody. "There's one spotlight. One. So why is the whole floor covered?"

Brody looked up. Each little mirror tile on the ball caught the beam and threw it somewhere different, so every tile made its own spot, and because the ball spun, the spots moved. One spotlight in, hundreds of moving spots out, because each mirror tile reflected the beam in a slightly different direction.

"Want me to demonstrate?" he said. He held up his phone with the flashlight on, angled it at his watch face, and a little white spot of light jumped onto the girl's sneaker. He tilted the watch a tiny bit and the spot slid away across the floor. She laughed.

"So the whole ball is just a bunch of watches," she said.

"A bunch of really organized watches."

The DJ started a song people actually liked, and the floor began to fill. The spots of light kept sweeping over everyone, faster now, like the room was breathing. The girl stuck out her hand.

"I'm Priya," she said. "That was the most fundamental thing anyone's said to me all night. Come on, you can explain the smoke machine next."

Brody put his phone in his pocket, where the group chat buzzed on, unread, and followed her onto the floor.

activity: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
knowledge_domain: the idea that prices rise when many people want something scarce and fall when it is plentiful
fact: The price at which the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers offer is called the equilibrium price, or market-clearing price.
story:
Jayden slid the last of his birthday money across his desk and counted it twice. Eleven dollars, and he needed three mangoes for the smoothie he was making Mom on Sunday, because she had said once, quietly, that mango smoothies tasted like a good day. At the grocery store he walked straight to the produce section and stopped cold. A small handwritten sign sat in an almost-empty bin: Mangoes, $2.50 each. He touched the sign as if it might be a mistake, but the plastic was cool and permanent. Two empty crates leaned against the wall behind the bin, and a stocker with a name tag that read ROSA was carrying the third away.

"There was a frost down south," Rosa said, not slowing down. "We get what we get." Jayden did the math in his head. Three mangoes would be seven fifty, which left him nothing for the orange juice, and without juice there was no smoothie, just a bowl of pulp. He stood there while a woman in a gray coat picked up four of the last six mangoes without even looking at the price. Four. Jayden watched her walk off and felt something click, a concept forming: lots of people wanted them, there weren't many, and the price was high. The three things went together.

That night his phone buzzed. A message from his friend Zoe: "Garage sale tomorrow on Elm. Mr. Ruiz is selling 20 skateboards he imported. Come early, it'll be huge." Jayden texted back that he was saving for mangoes, and Zoe replied, "That's the boringest sentence anyone has ever sent me." But he went anyway, because Zoe said the skateboards were five dollars each, and five dollars for a skateboard was like finding money on the ground.

It did not go how Zoe promised. At nine in the morning Mr. Ruiz's driveway was crowded, but his sign said twelve dollars, and people picked up the boards, looked at the price, and set them back down. By ten there were still fifteen skateboards, and Mr. Ruiz had crossed out the twelve and written nine. By noon only six were left, and the sign said seven. Zoe bought one and Jayden hung around to watch Mr. Ruiz change the sign one more time, to five fifty, and the last boards vanished in under twenty minutes. Not one left over, and not one buyer who walked away wanting one. "My son taught me that," Mr. Ruiz said, sweeping the empty driveway. "He says the price where the amount buyers want equals the amount sellers have is called the equilibrium price. Also market-clearing, because it clears you out exactly."

Sunday morning Jayden walked back to the grocery store. The mango bin was full, stacked into a wobbly orange pyramid, and Rosa was squeezing past crates of them. The sign read $1.25 each. His pulse seemed to accelerate as he grabbed three, then the orange juice, then paid with money to spare. The price had come down to meet the buyers, and it felt stable now, the way Mr. Ruiz's five fifty had felt, like the exact right number sitting still.

He carried the bag home and put everything on the counter, then set the leftover four dollars beside the blender. "That's for next time," he said, and got out the knife.

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Airliner cabins are pressurized, but under regulations the cabin air pressure may be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet (about 2,400 meters) above sea level.
story:
Theodore discovered the disaster the moment he unzipped his backpack on the train. Crumbs everywhere. His bag of salt-and-vinegar chips had burst along the seam sometime during the flight from Denver, and now his paperback, his headphones case, and even his spare socks were saturated with grease and shattered chip pieces. His little sister Maya leaned over from her window seat and burst out laughing.

"It's not funny," Theodore said, fishing out the limp, exploded bag. "I packed it sealed. It was fine at home. Then we get on the plane, and somewhere over the mountains it just blew up." He turned the bag over in his hands, frowning at it. Maya stopped laughing, because she could tell he was in one of his figuring-it-out moods, and those usually ended with something interesting.

"Remember the pretzel bag I bought in the airport?" she said. "The lady at the shop had to squeeze it into my tote because it was so stiff and puffed up. I thought she'd overfilled it."

Theodore pulled the crumpled in-flight magazine out of the side pocket of his backpack, where he had shoved it before landing. He flipped through it, past the maps and the duty-free pages, until he found the paragraph he had half-noticed during the flight. He read it aloud slowly. "Airliner cabins are pressurized, but under regulations the cabin air pressure may be as low as it would be at 8,000 feet, about 2,400 meters, above sea level." He looked up. "Eight thousand feet. That's like being on a tall mountain, even though the plane is way higher than that."

"So the air outside the bag, inside the cabin, gets thin," Maya said, catching on. "But the air inside the bag was sealed in back home, at normal pressure. So the bag puffs out, and if it's already full of chips, it pops."

Theodore grabbed his notebook. "We can test it," he said. "There was some controversy at school last month when Mr. Reyes said planes aren't really sealed like spaceships, and half the class didn't believe him. Conventional wisdom says the cabin is just like sea level, but it isn't, not exactly." He wrote out the plan in his careful block letters: one fresh sealed bag of chips in the backpack, one in the carry-on, checked at takeoff, mid-flight, and landing. If his idea was right, both bags would puff up hard somewhere over the ocean on the way home, then go soft again after they landed.

Their mom, who had been pretending to read her novel across the aisle, handed them a bag of peanuts without a word. Maya held it up. "Sealed at the factory," she said. "Want to save it for the flight home?" Theodore took it and tucked it into the front pocket of his backpack, right next to the notebook, and wrote one more line at the top of the page: Peanut bag, trial number one.

activity: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
knowledge_domain: the idea that posts, photos and location data can be stored, shared and seen by strangers
fact: Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and its Wayback Machine lets anyone look at old versions of many websites.
story:
The group chat lit up at 4:32 on a Tuesday. Marisol sent a screenshot of an old blog with a purple background and a clipart frog in the corner, followed by three crying-laughing emojis. "WAIT," she typed. "This is Dani's blog from third grade. It's still ONLINE."

Jonathan tapped the link. Sure enough, there was Dani's handwriting, scanned in, a whole page about her dream of owning forty-two hamsters. Below the frog, small gray letters said the page had been saved by something called the Wayback Machine. "What is that," he typed, "a time machine for frogs?"

"It's real," Dani answered, and he could tell from her short replies that she was not laughing. "Since 1996 the Internet Archive has been saving copies of public web pages, and anyone can look at old versions of sites. My mom just showed me. That's how Marisol found it."

Marisol apologized right away, typing fast. Jonathan scrolled down the old page instead. Near the bottom, under a post about the class talent show, Dani had written her old address and a map to her house so friends could come to her birthday party. Forty-two hamsters, he thought, and one home address, sitting in an archive where anybody could read it.

He remembered his own post from last spring, the video of his dog Biscuit in the backyard, with the school name visible on his gym shirt in the background. He had deleted the video in June. He typed to the chat: "Meet me in the library computer lab tomorrow. I want to test something." Then, because it was Dani's page that started this, he added, "Bring that link. I want to see how far back it goes."

The next day, four of them crowded around one screen. They opened the archive and searched for Dani's blog. There it was, captured over and over, year after year, like a photo album nobody had asked for. Jonathan felt his stomach go quiet. "So deleting doesn't really delete," he said. "If a page was public, a copy might live there anyway." He tried to mimic the casual voice of someone who had known this all along, but nobody was fooled. Marisol put her hand on the back of his chair.

He pulled up his own deleted video account next, searching in a systematic way, page by page, checking dates. Not there. He let out a breath, then stopped himself, because Dani was still staring at her old address on the screen. He slid the keyboard toward her. "You could write to them," he said. "There's a contact page."

That night Dani sent the group a photo of the message she had submitted, asking politely if the page could be taken down. Two days later came her reply: "It's gone. And my new blog has hamsters, no frogs, and no addresses." Jonathan typed back, "Forty-two hamsters deserves a fresh page."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: An opinion supported with evidence is still an opinion, but it is a more convincing one than an opinion given with no reasons.
story:
Gabrielle slid a folded paper across the dinner table, past the mashed potatoes, until it stopped against her brother Marcus's glass of milk. "Read the first line," she said.

Marcus picked it up with his fork hand. "'The city should paint a crosswalk at Fifth and Maple.'" He lowered the paper. "That's your opinion. The council gets a hundred of those a week."

"It's not just an opinion." Gabrielle pulled a crumpled notebook from her backpack and opened it to a page covered in tally marks. "I sat at that corner after school on Tuesday and Thursday. I counted eleven times when somebody almost got hit because there's no place to cross. Eleven near-misses in two days."

Their dad set down his serving spoon. "You counted near-misses? For how long?"

"Forty minutes each time." She tapped the tallies. "So when I say the city should paint a crosswalk, it's still my opinion, right? But an opinion with evidence behind it is more convincing than one with no reasons at all. Marcus's opinion is just words. Mine has eleven tallies."

Marcus frowned at the notebook. "Fine, it's more convincing than mine. But the council meeting is tomorrow at four. That's your deadline, right? You need signatures tonight."

"That's the problem." Gabrielle pushed her peas around her plate. "I thought I'd get spontaneous support, people just signing because it's obviously dangerous. But Mrs. Okafor next door said no. She wants proof. And I have proof, I just don't know if it's enough to sustain a whole argument, or if it's only a start."

"What else could you count?" her dad asked.

Gabrielle stared at the tally marks, then out the dark window toward the corner she couldn't see. She wondered whether more cars sped up on that stretch than on Oak Street, and whether you could even measure that without a radar gun. What about the number of kids who crossed there every day because the bus stop is on the wrong side? She flipped to a clean page and started writing questions faster than her handwriting could keep up.

"Slow down," Marcus said, watching her. "You have until four tomorrow, not four tonight."

"The bus comes at 7:10 tomorrow morning." Gabrielle was already standing, notebook in hand, chair scraping back. "If I'm there before school, I can count every kid who crosses. Then I'll have two kinds of proof."

She ran for the stairs, then stopped halfway and turned around. "Marcus, bring your watch. I need someone to time the forty minutes."

He sighed and drained his milk. "Fine. But you're carrying the clipboard."

activity: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
knowledge_domain: planting a vegetable garden and watching it grow
fact: A common gardening rule of thumb is to plant a seed about two to three times as deep as the seed is wide.
story:
Isabelle knelt on the concrete floor of Messina's Garden Center, a paper packet of carrot seeds in one hand and a packet of bean seeds in the other. The rules for the community plot said every vegetable had to be in the ground by Sunday, and today was Friday. She shook a carrot seed onto her palm, where it sat like a fleck of dust, then shook out a bean seed, fat as her fingertip.

"These can't go in the same depth," she said to her friend Marcus, who was hauling a bag of soil toward the register. "Look at them."

He set the bag down and peered at her hand. "The bean is like ten times bigger."

Isabelle turned the seed packets over, hunting for instructions. The carrot packet said "sow shallowly," which told her almost nothing. The bean packet said "plant two inches deep," but when she checked a carrot packet from another rack, that one just said "keep moist." She frowned at the shelf, where packets were sorted by category, and pulled out a radish packet, a pea packet, and a sunflower packet too.

"Okay, listen," she said, laying the packets in a row on the floor. "Big seeds say deep. Little seeds say shallow. Radish, tiny seed, half an inch. Pea, pretty big, one inch. Sunflower, huge, two inches." She tapped each packet. "So there's a rule hiding in here."

"Like the seed tells you how deep to bury it?" Marcus asked.

"Plant a seed about two to three times as deep as the seed is wide," Isabelle read aloud. She had found it on a laminated card hanging from a hook by the seed rack, worn soft at the corners from people thumbing it. "That's the rule. The bean is about an inch wide, so two or three inches down. The carrot seed is barely anything, so barely any dirt on top."

They carried their bags out to the community plot behind the garden center, where the air smelled of wet earth and cut grass. Isabelle measured with her finger, pressing the bean seeds into holes about three knuckles deep, then scattered the carrot seeds and dusted them with the thinnest layer of soil, thin as salt on fries. Marcus dug the fence posts for the pole beans, because raccoons, nocturnal thieves that they were, had emptied three plots last summer. The plot committee would not permit any harvest from unfenced beds.

Every morning before the bus, Isabelle walked over to check. On the fourth day, a haze of green threads showed where the carrots slept, so fine she almost breathed them away. The beans took longer, and she worried she had buried them too deep, until the eighth morning when fat hooked stems shouldered up through the soil like divers surfacing.

Marcus crouched beside her, mud on his knees, grinning at the bean sprouts. "So the little ones and the big ones both made it."

"Both came up," Isabelle said, and she traced a careful circle in the dirt around the strongest carrot seedling, marking it with a Popsicle stick.

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: Blue-enriched light from phone screens can reduce or delay the body's release of melatonin, the hormone that makes you sleepy in the evening.
story:
Emmett slid the phone box across the kitchen table, but his mother held her palm over it. "Rules first," she said. The lamplight caught the syrup bottle and the folded newspaper, relics of a Saturday breakfast that had ended an hour ago.

"One hour on school nights," she said. "It charges in the kitchen at bedtime, not in your room." Emmett argued that everyone in seventh grade took their phones to bed, and she argued back that she wasn't everyone's mother, and that after the recession had chewed through their savings, a phone at all was a gift they'd had to be frugal to manage. That word landed on him like a wet towel. He stopped trying to justify keeping it upstairs and signed the paper she pushed toward him, a contract with his own shaky signature.

For five nights the phone sat in the kitchen drawer at bedtime, and for five nights Emmett fell asleep within minutes of his head hitting the pillow. He didn't notice anything, because there was nothing to notice. On Friday night his mother was out, and he crept downstairs, opened the drawer, and lay on the couch in the dark scrolling through videos until nearly midnight. When he finally climbed the stairs, his eyes felt like they'd been rinsed in cold soda, wide awake behind his lids. He lay in bed listening to the furnace tick, counting to five hundred, then starting over. His sister's slow breathing came through the wall. Two o'clock. Then almost three.

At breakfast he fell asleep sitting up, his cheek drifting toward the cold table. His sister poked his arm. "What did you do last night?" she asked, and he told her, defensive at first, then quieter, because a pattern was forming in his head like dots on graph paper. Dark room plus no phone equaled sleep. Dark room plus glowing screen equaled staring at the ceiling for hours. "It's the screen," he said slowly. "It only happens on screen nights."

"You want to know the word for what you messed up?" his sister said, chewing. "Melatonin. It's the hormone that makes you sleepy." She said their science teacher had explained that blue-enriched light from screens can reduce or delay melatonin being released in the evening, and Emmett had been bathing his eyes in it until midnight.

Saturday night he put the phone in the drawer himself, before anyone asked. He set his alarm the old way, on the clock radio shaped like a rocket, and lay in the dark listening to his own breathing slow down, the hallway light a thin gold line beneath his door. From downstairs, faintly, came the drawer sliding shut, his mother's hand, then nothing at all.

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: USDA guidance says thawed freezer food can be safely refrozen if it still contains ice crystals or is at 40 degrees Fahrenheit (4 degrees Celsius) or below.
story:
The lights went out at 7:42, and Eve knew the exact time because she had been watching the clock, counting the minutes until her cupcakes came out of the oven. The oven went dark too, along with the refrigerator, the hallway light, and the whole city block outside the window. Her little brother Theo crawled out from under the kitchen table with a flashlight and nominated himself Chief of Darkness, which meant he got to hold the flashlight and shine it wherever he wanted.

The real problem, as Eve saw it, was the freezer. Mom was stuck at work until ten, and the note on the counter said leftovers, chicken, peas, be careful. Eve stood in front of the closed freezer door and reasoned it out. Cold air sinks, she thought, so every time someone opened the door, the coldest air spilled out the bottom like water from a cracked glass. The rule she made up was simple: nobody opens the freezer, not even Chief of Darkness, not even to check. Theo agreed, mostly because Eve let him nominate the flashlight as an official member of their alliance against the blackout.

They ate crackers and cheese on the living room floor and watched the building across the street, where some apartments still glowed with candlelight. Theo asked questions about whether the ice cream would melt, and Eve said she didn't know yet, which was the honest answer. She put her hand flat on the freezer door now and then, as if she could feel through the porous old seal, but of course she couldn't. What was happening inside was invisible, and she hated that.

At 9:15 the lights came back, all at once, and the refrigerator hummed like it had never stopped. Mom arrived twenty minutes later with a phone in her hand and worry in her face. "How long was it off?" she asked, and Eve told her, an hour and a half. Mom bit her lip. "The chicken. If it's thawed, it has to go."

"Wait," Eve said, and pulled out the bag of chicken. It was still hard as a brick, with frost on the plastic. Then she took out the peas and opened the bag so Mom could see. Inside, among the loose green dots, tiny ice crystals glittered in the kitchen light.

"Look," Eve said. "Still ice crystals. I found it on the food safety site while the power was out, on my phone. Thawed food can be refrozen if it still has ice crystals, or if it's forty degrees Fahrenheit or below."

Mom felt the chicken with her fingers, then held the phone and read the whole line herself, including the part about four degrees Celsius. "Alliance of the freezer," she said, and held up her hand for a high five. Theo shined the flashlight on the peas one more time, like a soldier inspecting his troops, and slid the bag back onto the shelf.

activity: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
knowledge_domain: tone differences, public versus private spaces and common conventions of online communication
fact: A small 2016 study by Binghamton University researchers found that text messages ending with a period were seen as less sincere than the same messages without one.
story:
Marcus's kitchen smelled like burned popcorn, and his mom was already laughing about it, so the two of them sat on the translucent glass porch table with the phone between them, watching the screen like it was a fishbowl. That was where Tyler had put it, face up, after Marcus threw it there.

"She's mad," Marcus said. "Look at it. She texted 'Okay.' and that's it."

"It says okay," Tyler said. "Okay is like the friendliest word there is."

"With a period." Marcus tapped the screen once, hard. "Kayla doesn't use periods. Kayla uses like forty emojis and the word 'okay' means fine. 'Okay.' means I'm dead to her."

Tyler picked up the phone and looked at the message again. Last month he'd sent his cousin "See you there." with a period, and his cousin had replied "why are you mad at me," and Tyler had spent a whole evening trying to figure out what he'd done wrong. Maybe nothing. Maybe it was the period itself. He couldn't see the difference, the way you couldn't see the start of an infection until the finger swelled up, but the difference was still in there, working.

"I read something," Tyler said. "A study. Binghamton University, 2016. Small one." He scrolled, found the page, held it out. "Same message, with a period and without. The one with the period came across as less sincere."

Marcus read it twice. "So I'm right."

"You're not right, you're a lab result. Let's test it." Tyler typed "that's cool" and sent it to Marcus's other phone, then sent "that's cool." right after. "Which one would make you panic?"

Marcus pointed at the second one without hesitating. "That one's cold. The first one's just talking."

"So to fix it with Kayla, you eliminate the period." Tyler deleted the period from a draft reply and turned the phone around. "Try this."

Marcus stared at the draft for a second. "Feels too easy."

"So send the emoji too," Tyler said. "Cover all the bases." He thought about his cousin again, about whether he should have just asked what was wrong instead of lying awake making up reasons. Maybe he'd message him tonight. Maybe with no period. Maybe with a whole parade of emojis.

Marcus hit send. The porch light buzzed, the popcorn smell drifted out through the screen door, and then Kayla's reply lit up the glass: "okay!! see you at 7" followed by a string of tiny dancing ghosts.

"There," Marcus said. "Saved. You're a genius."

Tyler slid the phone back across the table. "I'm going to go fix my cousin," he said.

activity: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
knowledge_domain: volunteering at a community food bank for the first time
fact: Gleaning means gathering crops left in fields after harvest, and some groups send volunteers to glean farms so the produce can go to food banks.
story:
Luke signed his name at the folding table outside the old hardware store, where the neighborhood cleanup had started at nine sharp. He wanted the volunteer hours for school, but he also wanted to matter, and a trash grabber seemed like a small way to matter. He worked the chain-link fence along the alley, pulling out a flattened soccer ball, a boot, and a strip of pink insulation that somebody had wedged between the fence posts, probably to block a gap. It crumbled in his hands and made him itch, so he dropped it in the bag fast.

By eleven, the pile of filled bags stood taller than he did. A woman in a green polo shirt backed a van up to the curb and started loading them, and Luke noticed the words on her shirt: Riverside Community Food Bank.

"You take the trash?" he asked.

"We take everything we can. The city drops the bags at the transfer station, and we compost the food scraps for the community garden." She held out her hand. "I'm Dana. You're the kid who did the whole fence line."

"Luke." He helped her lift the last bag, and then, because the van was still half empty, he asked what else went in it. She told him she was heading back to the food bank to shelve Saturday's delivery. "Sweet potatoes," she said. "A whole bin of them."

Luke frowned. "Where do sweet potatoes come from in October? Nobody around here grows them."

"Want to come see? We need hands tomorrow morning."

He rode along. The food bank occupied a low building with a loading dock and shelves that looked like a grocery store, except everything was free. Dana showed him where the canned goods went, then pointed to a bin of sweet potatoes with dirt still on them. "Saturday morning we go out to the Hartwell farm. You in?"

Luke said yes before he really thought about it. On the drive home that night, though, he turned the problem over. The bin had been full. Farmers sold their crops. Why would a farmer hand over perfectly good sweet potatoes to strangers? He was pessimistic about the whole thing, and he decided he would test it the only way he could: he would go, watch, and count.

Saturday morning the field was brown and stubbled. A machine had already gone through, and at first Luke saw nothing but dirt. Then he spotted one, half buried like a stone. Then three more within a step. The harvester couldn't get every potato, and the ones it missed were still good. He filled a bucket, then another.

Dana knelt beside him with her own bucket. "It's called gleaning," she said, "gathering what's left in the field after harvest."

"And it all goes to the food bank?" Luke asked.

"Every bit. Mr. Hartwell calls us when the machine's done, and we send volunteers out."

Luke counted his buckets. Eleven, by noon, and that was just him. The truck took them back, and at the food bank he helped Dana integrate the new sweet potatoes into the produce section, sliding them in beside the onions so the shelf looked full.

A woman came through the line with two kids and took a bag of them. Luke watched her put them in her cart, and then he grabbed one more bucket from the stack by the door and headed back to the truck.

activity: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
knowledge_domain: to prepare for a coming-of-age ceremony by learning a reading or prayer by heart
fact: A Torah scroll is written without vowels or musical marks, so a bar or bat mitzvah student learns the chanted melody of their reading in advance from a printed book.
story:
Anna sat cross-legged on the worn rug in her grandmother's living room, a practice book open on her knees. In three weeks she would chant from the Torah for her bat mitzvah, and her portion looked back at her like a puzzle: Hebrew letters in neat columns, tiny vowel dots below them, and curling symbols stacked above and below like musical birds on wires.

"You have the ambition," her grandmother said, setting down two glasses of mint tea, "now you need the patience." Anna traced one of the little curls with her finger. "What are these marks, Savta? They weren't in the email Rabbi Feld sent." Her grandmother just smiled and said Anna would find out herself at Thursday rehearsal, which felt like being handed a wrapped box and told not to open it.

All week Anna tested an idea. She covered the vowel dots with a strip of paper and tried to read a verse cold. The letters sat there, silent and stubborn. When she uncovered the dots and chanted the melody from the marks above, the words flowed again. So the little birds carried the tune, she reasoned, and the dots carried the sounds. Both of them were her crutches. What would happen if she had to read without crutches? The question itched.

On Thursday, in the sanctuary that smelled of wax and old wood, Rabbi Feld unrolled the Torah scroll on the long desk. Anna leaned over it and her stomach dropped. No vowel dots. No curling birds. Nothing but bare letters marching in parallel columns, the same words she had practiced, stripped of every clue she'd leaned on. "Where did the marks go?" she whispered.

"They were never there," Rabbi Feld said. "The scroll is written without vowels or musical marks."

Anna stared at the bare letters. So that was why her practice book existed at all. She had assumed the book was a convenience, a softened copy for kids. Now she understood it was the opposite: the only place the tune lived. She had to carry the melody and the vowels in her head before she ever touched the scroll. Every night until the ceremony, she would be negotiating between her eyes, which wanted the dots, and her memory, which had to supply them.

She went back to her grandmother's house and tried again with the paper strip, covering the vowels, then covering the melody marks, then both, chanting louder each time. Her grandmother turned the pages of her own book in the corner chair, tapping her foot to Anna's rhythm.

On the third try, the whole verse came out whole and unaided, rising and falling in the right places. Anna lifted the strip of paper like a flag. "Did you hear that?" she said. "No marks. All me."

activity: falling out with a best friend and making up
knowledge_domain: falling out with a best friend and making up
fact: A 2015 study that followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade found that friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end.
story:
Elena stared at her phone in the kitchen, waiting for Priya to reply. Three days now, and nothing, not even the eye-roll emoji. They used to text forty times a day. Then Priya made the soccer team and Elena joined robotics, and somehow the replies got shorter and slower until they stopped coming at all. Elena typed "u up?" into their thread, deleted it, and opened the family group chat instead, because if she kept watching the empty thread she was going to throw her phone into the sink.

"Question for the group," she posted. "How do you fix a friendship that's already broken?" Her dad replied with a thumbs up and the words "have you tried apologizing," which was useless. Her grandmother sent a voice memo, and Elena played it while stirring her after-school snack. "In my day we wrote letters," Grandma said, "and I'll tell you, the friendships that lasted were the ones where we stayed similar. When Terez and I got different jobs, that was the end." Her cousin Marco, who was in college, replied next: "Actually there's real research on this. A 2015 study followed 573 friendships formed in seventh grade. Friends who were less alike were more likely to see the friendship end."

Elena sat with that. She and Priya had been practically the same person in seventh grade, both obsessed with the same dumb cartoon, both terrible at dodgeball. Now they were less alike. So maybe the silence wasn't because Priya was mad. Maybe it was just the pattern doing what patterns do. She thought of her uncle, who owned a building downtown, always saying a good tenant helped the whole place thrive, but a volatile one could ruin everything, and the landlord had to act fast either way. Elena decided to act. If being less alike was the problem, then the fix wasn't to apologize for nothing. The fix was to find something new they both still cared about.

She scrolled back through months of Priya's messages looking for it, hunting for a topic that had survived the teams and the clubs. There. Eleven months ago Priya had gone on for two full screens about a mural going up near the library, the artist, the colors, everything. Elena had barely answered at the time because she'd been cramming for a math test. She opened a news app, found out the artist was painting another one this Saturday, and typed: "the mural artist you liked is doing a new one by the library sat. want to go watch and judge it really loudly?"

The typing bubble appeared. It disappeared. It appeared again. Elena held her breath so hard she got dizzy.

"I thought you were mad at ME," Priya wrote. "I was mad at YOU," Elena sent back, then: "we're both idiots." The reply came fast: "obviously. saturday. I'll bring snacks, you bring the loud judging." Elena dropped the phone on the counter and did a small, embarrassing victory spin in the kitchen, and behind her the group chat lit up with her grandmother writing, "so did my advice work."

activity: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
knowledge_domain: the difference between an opinion and a claim that can be checked
fact: Confirmation bias is the tendency to accept claims that fit what we already believe and to doubt claims that do not, without checking either.
story:
Dex slammed his backpack onto the bench and slid into his spot at the table before Mom had even set down the lasagna. "You guys hear about Ridgemont's point guard? Flunked his math class, so he's off the roster for the playoffs." He tore a piece of bread in half, grinning. "Their whole season is toast."

Nora's fork stopped halfway to her plate. If it was true, her school's team, who had lost to Ridgemont twice this year, might actually have a shot at the city title. "Who told you?"

"Marcus heard it from some kid at the arcade."

"That's like four people away from anyone who knows anything," Nora said, though a warm, satisfying feeling was already spreading through her chest. Of course the guy was failing. Ridgemont players were exactly the type.

Mom sprinkled parmesan on her pasta and said she'd believe it when she saw it, since her commute home ran past Ridgemont and there had been players shooting on the outdoor courts, same as always. Nora ignored that. She wanted the story to be true, so it felt true, like a sweater that already fit.

That night, in her room, she pulled up the league website on her laptop, telling herself it would take two minutes. The site posted eligibility lists every Friday. She scrolled, chewing the inside of her cheek, and found the current roster. The point guard's name was still there, plain as anything. Then she checked the stats page, where the league listed every player's scoring next to the median for the whole league. He was three points above the median and playing Friday night against her school. She sat back, the warm feeling gone, replaced by something colder. She had repeated the story at lunch today to two friends, confidently, and she hadn't checked a single thing. She'd just believed it because it fit what she already thought about Ridgemont. In science class there was a poster about exactly this, and now she said the phrase out loud to her dark ceiling: "Confirmation bias."

The next morning she caught Dex at the bus stop. "That thing about the point guard isn't true. He's on the roster, and he's playing Friday."

Dex squinted at her. "You actually looked it up? Man, don't be so gullible about Marcus."

"I was gullible," Nora said. "I believed it because I wanted it to be true. That's the whole trick of it." She pulled out her phone and showed him the eligibility list, then made him watch while she texted the two friends she'd told: not true, sorry, I checked the league site.

At dinner that night, Mom asked how the lasagna was, and Dex shrugged and said the point guard had dropped thirty points on their team, so thanks a lot, Nora. She laughed so hard she nearly knocked over her water glass. "Next time I'll hope for a better rumor," she said, and speared another piece of lasagna.

activity: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
knowledge_domain: the idea that people interpret the same events and ideas differently
fact: Akira Kurosawa's 1950 film Rashomon tells one crime through four witnesses whose accounts contradict each other.
story:
The vase had been on the mantel since before Abigail was born, and by Sunday dinner it was in six pieces on the floor. Everyone in the kitchen had a different story. Her older brother Marcus said the cat knocked it off while chasing a moth. Her grandmother insisted the shelf had been wobbling for weeks and it was bound to fall. Her little cousin Theo, still catching his breath, said he only touched it with one finger, just one, and it jumped. Aunt Rosa blamed the draft from the open window. Four stories, one broken vase, and no way to check any of them, because the cat was asleep, the moth was gone, and the window was shut now.

Abigail kept quiet through dinner, turning the pieces over in her mind. In class on Friday, Mr. Okafor had mentioned a film, and she had written the name in her notebook: Rashomon, from 1950. A boy named Daniel had leaned over and said, "It's a crime told four times, by four witnesses, and every version contradicts the others." She hadn't thought much of it then. Now she did.

On Monday, during the class discussion, she raised her hand. "I want to test something," she said. "This weekend a vase broke at my house. I got four stories and they can't all be true." Mr. Okafor tilted his head, and she hurried on before he could speak. "I think it matters who tells each story. So I made a chart." She held up her notebook. "Theo is the only one who was alone in the room right before it broke. Marcus blamed the cat, but the cat was locked in the basement all afternoon, because Grandma is allergic. Grandma blamed the shelf, but I checked, and it's solid." She paused, and the room went still. "Aunt Rosa blamed the wind, but the window was only open for two minutes, and it faces away from the room."

"Which leaves Theo," Daniel said slowly.

"I didn't say that," Abigail answered, though she had thought it hard all Sunday night. "Theo said he touched it with one finger. That's actually the most plausible story, because it's the only one where the teller makes himself look worse, not better."

"That's exactly the Rashomon problem," Daniel said. "Everyone shades the story."

"It's more than shading," Abigail said. "Every candidate had a reason. Marcus didn't want to be blamed for leaving the basement door open. Grandma didn't want Theo crying at dinner. Aunt Rosa likes a mystery." She tapped her chart. "Nobody lied, exactly. They just saw different true things."

Mr. Okafor asked what she thought actually happened. Abigail looked down at her notebook, then up.

"Theo touched it, the shelf was fine, the cat was downstairs. I asked him last night, just us two, no audience. He said, 'It was warm from the sun and I just wanted to hold it.'"

The class was quiet, and Abigail closed her notebook gently, like the vase was still whole inside it.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: In a fair test, everything except the variable being tested is kept the same, such as the amount, the temperature and the timing.
story:
Kaitlyn crouched between the tomato rows with her notebook open on her knee, and the tomato on the healthy plant stared back at her like it knew something she didn't. Two rows, same seeds, same soil, planted the same afternoon in April. The left row stood tall and green. The right row drooped, its leaves curling under like old paper. Something invisible was at work, and she intended to find out what.

Her first guess was water. "It's a hypothesis," she told her little brother, Danny, when he wandered over with a popsicle. "A testable guess. I have one, and I'm going to test it."

"Sounds trivial to me," Danny said, working on the popsicle with great concentration. "They're plants. They droop. Big deal."

The bee numbers were down this year, everyone at the garden said so, the whole population in a recession, and Kaitlyn had already ruled out pollination, since the bees that did show up seemed happy to pollinate both rows equally.
