It wasn't the bees. She was almost sure it was the water, since the drooping row sat closer to the fence, where the sprinkler's arc might fall short.

So she tested it. She dragged a watering can down the droopy row every morning, a good soaking, and within a week the plants perked up. Case closed, she wrote in her notebook. Except they didn't stay perked. They sagged again, worse, and one of them turned yellow at the bottom. Kaitlyn stood there feeling like the notebook had lied to her.

Then she noticed the hose. Her mother had been rinsing the compost bin on the far side of the fence, and the runoff pooled near the drooping row every evening, standing in a low, sunken patch of ground. Kaitlyn's extra morning watering had landed on top of evening runoff, and the sick row was sitting in mud while the healthy row drained fine. Too much water, not too little. Her test had told her the wrong answer, and she wanted to know why. She looked at her notebook, then at the two rows, and saw it. In her test, the two rows had not been treated the same except for the water. The sick row also had the sunken ground, the afternoon shade from the fence, and the runoff. Everything was different, so the test had proved nothing at all.

She started over with two pots of the same seeds, same size, same soil from the same bag, set side by side on the flat part of the patio where the shade fell evenly. Same amount of water, measured to the line on a jar. Same spot, so the temperature stayed the same for both. Same timing, morning and morning, seven o'clock sharp, because that was the part Danny was in charge of, and Danny took the job suspiciously seriously for someone who called the whole project trivial. Two weeks later one pot stood green and the other, the one she'd doubled the water for, drooped in exactly the curling-paper way.

She wrote a single line at the bottom of the page and turned the notebook toward Danny. "Same amount, same temperature, same timing, everything the same except the one thing I'm testing," she read out loud. "And now the answer's actually the answer."

Danny licked the last of his popsicle off the stick. "So it was too much water all along?"

"It was too much water all along," Kaitlyn said, and closed the notebook with a snap.

activity: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
knowledge_domain: persuasion techniques such as bandwagon appeals, loaded words and celebrity testimonials used in ads and propaganda
fact: In the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something.
story:
Aurora had sixty-two dollars in her pocket and one hour before her mom picked her up at the food court, and she intended to spend both on the new Drift sneakers everyone at school was suddenly wearing. She had saved since March, skipping the fall festival and two movie nights, and last week she had even told her grandmother the money was for "plumbing repairs" on her locker, which still made her wince when she thought about it. She crossed the shiny tile floor toward the shoe store, past a kiosk where a sign shouted, "The hoodie EVERYONE is talking about!" Above it, a TV screen showed the rapper Zay Marlow holding up the same hoodie and saying it was the softest thing he'd ever worn. Aurora slowed down. She had almost bought that hoodie in September, until she saw the price.

Inside the shoe store, the Drifts glowed on a backlit wall like something holy. A banner read "LIMITED. LEGENDARY. LOVED BY MILLIONS." She turned a display box and found Zay Marlow's face on that too, grinning, with the words "Zay says: unstoppable." Last month she would have carried the box straight to the register. But something had changed after Saturday, when she was scrolling reviews for a phone case she wanted.

She'd been watching a girl named FoxiiBee raving about the case, calling it flawless, calling it life-changing, and Aurora had been one tap from buying when she noticed the tiny "#ad" in the caption. She'd looked it up, frowning at her phone in the kitchen, and learned that in the United States, the Federal Trade Commission requires influencers and celebrities to clearly disclose when they were paid or given free products to promote something. She'd scrolled back through three more of FoxiiBee's videos. Two had the tag. The video for the phone case did not, and neither did a blurry story that said "gifted!!" with no other marking.

Now, in the store, she asked a clerk with a silver nose ring, "Does Zay Marlow actually buy these shoes, or did Drift just send them to him?" The clerk laughed. "They send him a whole pallet. He's under contract. There's supposed to be a disclosure somewhere, you know, so it complies with the FTC rule. It's on their website, I think, in tiny print." Aurora picked up the box and studied the back, angling it so it sat perpendicular to the shelf edge, letting the light catch the fine print near the barcode. There it was, smaller than the size chart: "Compensated endorsement."

She stood there weighing the shoes in her hands. They were well made; she could feel that. Millions of people did love them, though that banner also told her exactly what the company wanted her to think. Maybe Zay liked them too. Maybe he'd have liked anything they paid him enough to like.

At the register, she set the box down and then, slowly, slid it back toward herself. "I'll take them," she said, "but I'm going to wear them because I like them, not because a rapper got a pallet." The clerk grinned and rang her up. As she walked out, she passed the hoodie kiosk again and shot the sign a look. "Everyone," she muttered, "except me."

activity: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
knowledge_domain: breaking an arm and wearing a cast
fact: As a broken bone heals, the body forms a callus, a mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends.
story:
Kaitlyn sat on the low wall by the swings, her right arm resting in its blue cast like something she was babysitting. Three weeks ago she had fallen off the monkey bars, and now she watched the bars from a distance, the way you might watch a dog that had bitten you. Her best friend Priya swung back and forth beside her, pumping her legs.

"You're staring again," Priya said.

"I'm not staring. I'm thinking." Kaitlyn turned the cast so the signatures faced the sun. Near her wrist, under the plaster, she could feel a firm lump she had noticed two days ago, a ridge that had not been there before. It worried her at first. Then she remembered the follow-up visit, when the doctor had held up the new X-ray against the light and pointed to a fuzzy shadow spanning the break. "That's your callus," he had said, and her mother had smiled, so Kaitlyn had figured it was a good thing. She'd read the report in the folder when nobody was looking: as a broken bone heals, the body forms a callus, a mass of cartilage and new bone that bridges the gap between the broken ends.

"Thinking about what?" Priya dragged her feet to stop the swing.

"About whether the lump means it's working in there. It's like a bridge being built where you can't see it. Cartilage first, then new bone." She pressed gently on the ridge through the cast. It did not hurt, which she decided was probably a good sign.

Priya hopped off the swing. "So if the bridge is halfway built, could you hang from the bars? Just for a second?"

"No. The doctor said no weight on it for six weeks."

"You could use just the left hand and sort of balance with the cast."

"Balance is a polite word for falling." Kaitlyn slid off the wall anyway and walked to the monkey bars, keeping a careful distance, like a scientist approaching a skunk. Priya followed, and by the time they reached the bars, half the fifth grade had gathered, because a kid in a cast near forbidden equipment is the most interesting thing a playground can offer.

"She's going to do it," a boy named Marcus announced.

"She's not," Kaitlyn said. "I came to look, not to swing." But she stood there measuring the distance with her eyes, and she had to admit her motivation was not entirely scientific. Part of her wanted to prove the bars hadn't won.

"Your arm won't cooperate even if you tried," Priya said. "It's still knitting."

Kaitlyn flexed her fingers inside the cast. They cooperated fine. That was the strange part. The fingers worked, the wrist was stiff but alive, and underneath it all, invisible crews were laying down cartilage and new bone across the gap, closing it a little more every day. She tried an experiment. She raised her left hand, gripped the first bar, and hung, letting the cast hang loose beside her, touching nothing. Her body swung. It felt almost like flying. Three seconds later she dropped down onto the wood chips, and the crowd groaned with disappointment.

"You didn't even try the cast hand," Marcus said.

"That was the experiment. One hand, no weight on the broken side. I'm not falling off these bars twice in one lifetime." She looked up at the row of rungs glinting in the afternoon light. Six weeks from now, when the cast came off, she would come back and cross every single bar.

Just then the bell rang, and everyone turned to run inside. Marcus, sprinting for the line, caught his sneaker on the edge of the wood-chip border and went down hard, holding his wrist, his face going pale.

Kaitlyn crouched beside him and did her best not to smile. "It hurts, right? Wrong place, wrong angle?"

"Really bad," Marcus whispered.

"Well, here's the good news. In about three weeks you'll feel a lump, and it means a bridge is going up in there." She patted her cast. "The bad news is I get the swing wall and the good seat at lunch for the next month, because that's how the cast club cooperates."

Marcus stared at her, then down at his swelling wrist, and said the words every kid on that playground was already thinking. "I should have stayed by the swings."

activity: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
knowledge_domain: to look at onion skin cells under a microscope and label the cell wall, membrane and nucleus
fact: A microscope's total magnification is the eyepiece power multiplied by the objective lens power, so a 10x eyepiece with a 40x objective magnifies 400 times.
story:
Paisley crouched between the tomato beds at the community garden, holding a slice of onion skin so thin she could almost see through it, like a scrap of cloudy glass. Mr. Ruiz had left the garden's old microscope on the picnic table before driving off to the hardware store, and Paisley wanted more than anything to see the cells before he came back. Her lab sheet had three empty blanks waiting for labels: cell wall, cell membrane, nucleus. She had never labeled anything under a microscope before, and she only had one shot at the prize for the summer science contest, a packet of heirloom seeds that everybody wanted.

Her friend Donte arrived on his bike, dropped it in the gravel, and peered over her shoulder. "My cousin said onion cells look like bricks in a wall," he said. "That's why they're easy to start on."

Paisley switched on the light and pressed her eye to the rubber eyepiece. The onion skin bloomed into view, a patchwork of little boxes, each one edged in a darker line. She drew a rectangle in her notebook and marked the outer edge. Cell wall. But where was the rest? Everything looked flat and faint, like a photograph underwater. "The nucleus should be a darker dot," she murmured. "Is it hiding, or is it just too small?"

"Maybe you need to turn it up higher," Donte said, squinting at the dial on the side. He spun the nosepiece until a longer lens clicked into place. "There. That one says forty."

Fifty times bigger sounded plenty to Paisley, but Donte shook his head. "It's the eyepiece times the objective," he said. "The top part says ten times, and this one says forty times, so it's four hundred times bigger, not fifty." Paisley lifted her head, checked the numbers stamped on both lenses herself, and did the multiplication on the corner of her page. Ten times forty was four hundred. Donte was right, and that meant her cells had been tiny ghosts before, too faint to hold a nucleus.

When she looked again, the patchwork sharpened. A pale dot floated near the center of one brick, and around it, just inside the dark wall, she could make out a thinner line hugging the edge like plastic wrap. Cell membrane. She labeled all three blanks, pressing hard enough to dent the paper, then taped the onion skin into her notebook to conserve it for the contest judges.

Donte leaned in for his turn, adjusted the fine focus with great care, and frowned. "Paisley. Are we sure these aren't the sinister ones?" He pointed at a cluster of cells near the edge of the skin, blotched and collapsed where her fingernail had squeezed too hard. "Looks like an infection got them." Paisley snatched back the notebook, but it was too late to salvage that corner. She grabbed the whole onion from the picnic table and started peeling off a fresh layer, layer after layer, saying, "Good thing onions have more skins than I have patience."

activity: going on a school field trip with the class
knowledge_domain: going on a school field trip with the class
fact: A dairy cow only produces milk after she has given birth to a calf.
story:
Jack had been looking forward to the aquarium field trip for weeks, mostly because it meant a whole day away from regular classes. He and his best friend Marcus claimed the seats at the back of the bus, and by the time they rolled into the parking lot, they had already planned to see the shark tunnel first, the octopus second, and the jellyfish room whenever they felt like wandering.

Near the entrance stood a trivia station with a big spinning wheel. A volunteer handed Jack a card. "Answer three questions right and you win a behind-the-scenes tour of the seal exhibit." Jack spun the wheel, which landed on what looked like a completely random category: Farm Facts. "Odd choice for an aquarium," the volunteer admitted, "but everybody eats, right? First question: true or false, every dairy cow in a milking barn has had a calf."

Jack opened his mouth to say false, because in his head cows just made milk all the time, like a faucet. Marcus elbowed him. "Guess," he whispered. Before Jack could, Priya, the quiet girl from his science class who almost never spoke on trips, stepped up beside him. "A dairy cow only produces milk after she has given birth to a calf," she said. "So it's true. Every one of them." Jack repeated her answer, the volunteer stamped the card, and they moved to the next question, which Jack got wrong, and the third, which Marcus got right.

"You know cows," Jack said to Priya as they collected their tour passes. She shrugged. "I live on a dairy farm. I've watched it my whole life." Jack felt his ears go warm. He had sort of assumed she was quiet because she didn't know much about anything fun, and that was a stereotype he hadn't even noticed he was carrying. He was about to resign himself to being the dumb one on this tour when Priya added, "Don't feel bad. Half my cousins argue with me about it at Thanksgiving."

Behind the scenes, the seal keeper led them past tanks and buckets of fish, and Jack actually asked questions, three in a row, and one of them made the keeper say, "Huh. Good eye." At the last tank, a silvery fish with a black stripe kept bumping the glass. "That one's totally random," Jack said. "Just swimming into the wall over and over."

"That's a kelp perch," Priya said. "They feed at the edge of things, right where the glass is." The keeper nodded, impressed, and Jack turned to Marcus. "Remind me to sit near Priya on the way home."

activity: getting a first pair of glasses
knowledge_domain: getting a first pair of glasses
fact: Astigmatism happens when the cornea or lens is slightly egg-shaped, curving more in one direction than the other, which blurs vision at any distance.
story:
Elena sat on the crinkly paper of the nurse's cot and squinted at the eye chart taped to the cabinet door. The top E was easy. The second line was a smear of gray. The third line might as well have been spilled ink.

"You failed the screening twice," Nurse Patel said. "The optometrist is already here for the sixth graders. Come on."

The optometrist's folding chair sat under the window, next to a rack of trial lenses. He flipped lenses in front of her eyes, one after another. "Read the line with the T."

"O, maybe D, then something with a tail."

"Better or worse?" He slid a new lens in.

"Better. The letters aren't smearing sideways anymore." Elena leaned forward. "Wait. Why did they smear? I thought you're either nearsighted or farsighted. My friend Marcus is nearsighted, and his stuff is blurry only far away. Mine's blurry everywhere."

"That's a different thing," the optometrist said. "It's called astigmatism."

"But what is it?" Elena asked, because Nurse Patel was no help and he kept flipping lenses.

He shrugged, already reaching for the next lens. "Your cornea, or maybe the lens inside the eye, is slightly egg-shaped. Curves more in one direction than the other. Blurs things at any distance."

Elena went still. An egg. She thought of the way light came through the porous curtain in her bedroom and stretched into ovals on the floor. If the curve was uneven, the light wouldn't land in one point. That would smear the letter sideways, near and far both, which was exactly what she'd been seeing since October, when the whiteboard turned to fog and she'd copied Marcus's notes out of desperation and felt a hot spike of resentment when he called her a cheater.

She had a theory to test. "Hold on. If it's egg-shaped, the blur should have a direction, right? The same direction everywhere?" She held up her hand and curled her fingers slightly, like a tunnel tilted one way. She looked at the chart through the gap. The letters stretched sideways. She tilted the gap the other way. They stretched the other way. "So a lens curved unevenly would smear the E left or right depending on which way the egg sits. Mine smears left. Every line, near and far."

The optometrist stopped flipping lenses and looked at her. "Try this one."

The third line snapped into focus. F, Z, B, D, 4. She read it clean to the bottom, and her eyes stung because she hadn't known letters had that many sharp edges.

Nurse Patel wrote something on a slip. "Glasses in a week."

"A week?" Elena said. "Can I at least keep the chart?"

activity: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
knowledge_domain: getting a first phone and learning to use it responsibly
fact: The first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by Motorola engineer Martin Cooper on a New York street on April 3, 1973.
story:
Charlotte slid the phone box across the kitchen table like it might explode, which, in a way, it already had, because her little brother had knocked over a glass of juice and the box had saved the table from a lake of purple.

"Careful, that's the whole reason we're still dry," she said, and Owen grinned like a supervillain.

Mom sat down with a slice of cold pizza, which was her way of making any ceremony feel less like a ceremony. "Okay. Ground rules before you turn it on."

"Twelve texts a day," Charlotte guessed.

"Use your brain, not a number," Mom said. "Rule one: nobody gets in trouble for telling me something weird that happened online. Rule two: the phone charges in the kitchen at night. Not your room. The kitchen."

"That's so you can check it," Charlotte said.

"No, it's so I can see the screen glow at two in the morning and know exactly which child to confiscate it from."

At the store that afternoon, a kid named Dev had been waiting behind them, bouncing on his heels, and he'd asked the salesman a question Charlotte couldn't stop thinking about: how long have people actually had phones in their pockets? The salesman had said the first call from a handheld cellular phone was made by a Motorola engineer named Martin Cooper, right on a New York street, on April 3, 1973. Dev had whispered, "Fifty years and my mom still calls me during class," and Charlotte had laughed so hard the display rack rattled.

Now she turned the phone over in her hands. Fifty-some years since Martin Cooper stood on that street. Her whole life, phones had just existed, like plumbing, invisible until something went wrong. She tried to picture a world where carrying one was brand new, where people on the sidewalk stared. It was like trying to picture the ocean before water.

"Are you having a trance?" Owen asked. "You look tranquil. It's creepy."

"I'm thinking about 1973." She set the phone down. "Okay, I want to test something. Rule one says tell you weird stuff. So here's weird: yesterday at school, before I even had this phone, some account named SunnyDeals42 started texting me on Mom's old tablet. It said I'd won something."

Mom put down her pizza. "What did it want?"

"A code. It said the prize would arrive once I confirmed my address." Charlotte spread her hands. "I didn't reply. But I was thinking, it knew my name. I never entered anything anywhere. So either someone gave it my name, or it's guessing names at random and waiting for somebody to say yes."

"That's called phishing," Mom said slowly. "You already did the right thing, and I'm not even going to pretend to be calm about how right you did it."

"I want to reply," Charlotte said.

"You what?"

"Not with real information. One word: nope. Then I watch what happens. If it gets pushy or weird, that proves it's a pattern, a machine hunting. If it writes back like a normal person, maybe it's a person. Either way we know more than we did."

Mom studied her for a long moment, then pushed the tablet across the table. "One word. That's it."

Charlotte typed nope and hit send. Eleven seconds later the reply landed: URGENT!!! PRIZE EXPIRES TONIGHT!!! CLICK HERE!!!

"Machine," they said at the same time, and Owen fell off his chair laughing.

"Blocked and reported," Charlotte said, feeling like Martin Cooper must have felt on that New York street, holding something that changed everything, except hers was slightly sticky from purple juice. "Mom. Can we look up what he actually said on that first call? Please tell me he said something cooler than nope."

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: The word Inuit means 'the people' in the Inuktitut language, and one person is called an Inuk.
story:
The banner over the community centre doorway read Heritage Festival, and Bennett slipped past a cluster of kids to evade the line forming at the entrance table. His project board was due by four o'clock, and the caption still wasn't finished. He carried it under one arm, the glue drying in streaks, the last line blank except for a pencil mark where a word should go.

The problem was Mr. Okafor's note, folded into Bennett's pocket: "Check your wording before you submit." Bennett knew which wording. His caption read: "Drummer and throat singer, performances by an Inuit." He had copied the phrase from a library book, but something about it had started to nag at him on the bus, the way a pebble in a shoe does.

Inside, the hall smelled of fried plantains and cardamom. A woman in a printed headwrap was explaining a wall of photographs to two teenagers: "We call ourselves Igbo," she said, "not tribe, if you can manage it." Nearby, a Scottish pipe band tuned up with a sound like an argument between geese. Bennett walked the aisles, half listening, half rehearsing what he might ask a stranger.

At the northern tables, a man was arranging carvings of seals and a kayak paddler. A card beside the display said Inuit Artists Collective. Bennett stood there a moment, then made himself speak. "Excuse me. I'm doing a school project. Is it right to say a performer is an Inuit, or is there another word?"

The man set down a carving of a loon. "Inuit means 'the people,'" he said. "So it works for the group. One person is called an Inuk." He tapped the card. "That's why it says Artists, not one name. You wouldn't say an Inuit any more than you'd say a the-peoples."

Bennett wrote it on his palm in letters he could still read: one person, an Inuk. The man showed him how the word sat in Inuktitut, sounds Bennett tried and mangled, and the man laughed, not unkindly, and said the second try was better.

At four o'clock exactly, Bennett propped his board on the submission table at the back of the hall, where a judge with a clipboard was already moving down the row. He uncapped his pen and, in his most assertive handwriting, printed the new caption: "Drummer and throat singer, performances by an Inuk and by Inuit from across the north." The pipes started up behind him, swelling toward what had to be the climax of their set, and the judge paused at his board, clipboard steady, and read the last line twice.

"Nice fix," she said. "Half the entries get that wrong."

activity: getting through an evening power cut at home
knowledge_domain: getting through an evening power cut at home
fact: A 2016 world atlas of light pollution estimated that about 80 percent of North Americans cannot see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light.
story:
The power died with an abrupt click at half past eight, right in the middle of Ryder's game, and the whole house at Grandpa's went black except for the thin gray line of the window curtains. Ryder sat very still and listened. No furnace hum, no refrigerator drone, nothing. From downstairs, Grandpa's voice drifted up the stairs, calm as ever. "Well. Guess the county's having fun tonight. Candles are in the sideboard, third drawer."

Ryder felt his way down, bumping his hip on the banister, and found Grandpa already striking a match in the kitchen. The flame caught, and Grandpa set a stubby candle on the counter, then another on the table, converting the bright, familiar kitchen into something from an old photograph, all shadows and warm little pools of light. "You okay on your phone?" Grandpa asked. "Dead," Ryder said. "I forgot my charger." He'd been planning to charge it at home tomorrow. Now the screen was a dark black rectangle, useless as a brick, and something in his chest tightened at that.

Grandpa took a long flashlight from the mudroom shelf and nodded toward the back door. "Come on. When I was a kid, blackout nights were the best ones. Let's see if they still are." Outside, the whole street was dark, every porch light and window out, and the sky above them was not the sky Ryder knew. It was crowded. There were so many stars it looked almost messy, a spilled bag of salt, and across the middle of it ran a pale, hazy river of light he had never once seen from any city or suburb in his life.

"That's the Milky Way," Grandpa said quietly. "Haven't seen it from this yard since I don't know when." Ryder kept staring. He kept thinking there must be something wrong with his eyes, some smudge on his glasses, but no, it was real, and it was enormous, and it had apparently been hanging over his head his entire life without him ever knowing. Then he remembered where he'd seen something about this, a library book about the night sky he'd flipped through last month and mostly ignored. He'd skipped the paragraphs and read only the fact boxes. One of them had stuck anyway. "There was this atlas," he said slowly. "A world atlas of light pollution, from 2016. It estimated about eighty percent of North Americans can't see the Milky Way from where they live, because of artificial light." He checked Grandpa's face to see if he'd remembered it wrong, but Grandpa just nodded.

"Go get my laser pointer," Grandpa said. "Top drawer of my desk, the little silver one." Ryder fetched it, and Grandpa thumbed it on and traced a slow line up the black sky, pointing out Vega, then Deneb, then the whole glowing river itself, the green beam looking almost like it touched the stars. Ryder wanted to test something. If all that glow in the sky was really stars that the streetlights normally drowned out, then a single porch light coming back on should erase at least part of it. He stood squinting at the Milky Way, waiting for some house somewhere to flicker back to life so he could watch the stars vanish in real time. Nothing came on. The whole neighborhood stayed dark, and the sky stayed crowded, and the wait itself felt like its own strange gift.

The streetlights snapped back on all at once around ten, so sudden that Ryder flinched, and the Milky Way disappeared like breath wiped off glass. Only a dozen of the brightest stars survived. He hadn't even gotten to finish his test, but he'd seen enough: the stars had been there the whole time, waiting behind the porch lights and the glowing windows, and all it took to hide an entire galaxy was ordinary electricity. He'd spent the whole evening mad about his dead phone, and now, staring up at the washed-out sky he used to think was normal, he couldn't decide whether he wanted the power back or not.

"Same time next blackout?" Grandpa said, pocketing the laser pointer. Ryder watched the porch light buzz and steady itself, steady and bright and ruinous. "Yeah," he said. "But I'm bringing a blanket."

activity: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
knowledge_domain: saying goodbye to a grandparent who has died
fact: The 1996 book 'Continuing Bonds' argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects or traditions, can be a healthy part of grieving.
story:
Lucas stood in the hallway outside room 412 with his grandfather's watch already on his wrist, though he could not remember deciding to put it there. His hand had gone to his back pocket for the tissue and come back with the watch instead, like a reflex he hadn't known he had. Inside the room, his grandmother was folding the blanket at the foot of the empty bed, smoothing it flat, then smoothing it again. The air smelled of antiseptic and the faint orange peel his grandfather had always kept in his shirt pocket, even in here, even at the end.

"Grandpa would've wanted you to have that," she said, nodding at the watch.

Lucas turned the cracked leather band with his thumb. Last summer his grandfather had caught him messing with it and smacked his hand away, laughing. Now nobody would smack his hand again, and that thought made his throat hurt. But something else bothered him too, a worry he couldn't shake. His school counselor had said the word "moving on" about his dog that died in fourth grade, and Lucas had gotten the idea stuck in his head that grief was like a hallway you walked down, and if you stopped to hold on to things, you never got out. Wearing the watch felt like stopping. He tested the idea quietly, taking the watch off and setting it on the bedside table, the way you might exclude a bad-luck charm from your pocket before a test. The room felt colder. He picked it back up.

While his grandmother signed papers at the nurses' station, Lucas wandered down to a small room with a sign that said FAMILY RESOURCE SHELF. He expected pamphlets with clip-art teddy bears, but the shelf held real books. One was thin and serious, nothing like the contemporary covers with bright cartoons in the bookstore, and the spine said Continuing Bonds, 1996. He pulled it down and read the back, mouthing the words. It said the book had argued that keeping a connection to someone who has died, through memories, objects, or traditions, could be a healthy part of grieving. He read it twice, then a third time, pressing the words into himself.

He carried it back down the hall, the watch ticking against his wristbone. "Grandma," he said, "did you know some people think you're supposed to keep stuff? Like wearing his watch isn't, like, cheating?"

She looked at the book, then at him, and something in her shoulders let go. "Continuing bonds," she said. "Your grandpa kept his own father's pocket knife in the garage drawer for forty years. Never sharpened a thing with it."

Lucas slid the book back onto the shelf outside room 412, where his grandmother was waiting with the car keys. He wound the watch the way he'd watched his grandfather do it a thousand times, crown between thumb and finger, slow, until it resisted. "Tuesday pancakes," he said. "Grandpa's recipe. You keep the buttermilk in the garage fridge, right?"

"Back shelf," she said, "behind the soda water." She took his hand, and they walked past the nurses' station toward the elevator doors, the watch ticking the whole way down.

activity: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
knowledge_domain: the idea of a hypothesis as a testable guess that an experiment can support or overturn
fact: Philosopher Karl Popper argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong.
story:
Every morning that week, Victoria found the kitchen floor wet in the same spot, a shallow puddle by the window above the sink. Her mother blamed her for spilling water. Victoria was tired of being blamed, and more than that, she wanted to know what was really happening, because nothing in the house leaked as far as anyone could tell.

She made a guess: condensation was forming on the cold water pipe that ran behind the wall, and it dripped down through a gap in the floorboards. It was a guess about something she could not see, since the pipe was hidden, so she needed a way to test it. If the pipe was the cause, she reasoned, the puddle should form even when nobody used the sink all night. She taped a paper towel over the gap in the boards, taped another to the wall near the window, and marked the spots with pencil so she could tell them apart.

The next morning both paper towels were dry and the puddle was back. Her guess about the pipe was wrong, and she said so out loud at breakfast, which surprised her brother, Dean, who was building an intricate model bridge out of toothpicks for his own project. "You sound happy your idea failed," he said. "It's not fun," Victoria said. "But at least I know something now." Dean looked up from his bridge, which had reached a plateau in its construction, and shrugged.

While hunting through the hall closet for a flashlight, Victoria found a box of her father's old college books. One, a battered paperback with a cracked spine, had a chapter with a sentence she read three times: a philosopher named Karl Popper had argued, in a book first published in 1934, that an idea is scientific only if some possible observation could prove it wrong. She carried the book to the kitchen and read the sentence to Dean. "So my pipe idea counted," she said. "There was a result, dry towels, that could knock it down. And it did."

"Then what's your next one?" Dean asked. Victoria looked at the window above the sink, at the puddle below it, and at the tarp-covered grill on the patio just outside. Her new guess was that dew was collecting on the tarp at night and running off its lowest corner, which hung a few inches above the window ledge. If that was true, the puddle should vanish if the tarp's corner was moved. It should also mean wet streaks on the ledge itself, which she had not checked.

That evening she slid the tarp's corner a foot to the left and propped it on a bucket, so any runoff would drip onto the patio stones instead. She set a cup on the window ledge to catch anything that touched it. Then she went to bed and lay awake for a while, turning the philosopher's rule over in her mind. An idea you could not test, she thought, was just something you liked believing.

In the morning the floor was dry. The cup on the ledge held half an inch of water, and the patio stones under the tarp's old corner were dark with moisture. Victoria called her mother into the kitchen and showed her the cup, the dry floor, and the sentence in the book, bookmarked with a toothpick. "I was wrong about the pipe, and I almost let you humiliate me about spilling," she said. "It was the grill tarp the whole time."

Her mother leaned over the cup and laughed. "So what do we do about it?" "Move the tarp for good," Victoria said, "or hang a gutter on it." She was already pulling on her boots to go outside and slide the whole tarp farther down the patio.

activity: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
knowledge_domain: the ways individuals and groups describe themselves, their heritage and their experiences of belonging
fact: Canada's census has let people report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, so the origin totals add up to more than the country's population.
story:
Sawyer spread his poster board on the folding table beside the samosa booth and frowned at his bar graph. He had counted the origins listed for his town on the census website, the same numbers his teacher had shown the class, and turned them into percentages. Scottish, eighteen percent. Chinese, fourteen. Cree, eleven. Métis, nine. Indian, eight. Ukrainian, seven. He added them twice on his calculator, and both times the total came out to ninety-seven percent, which would have been fine, except he still had six more bars to count. By the end he was at a hundred and forty-three percent, which was impossible. People did not just appear out of nowhere, and the festival around him was proof: the whole town square was booths and flags and food steam, maybe two thousand people, definitely not two thousand eight hundred and sixty.

He decided to test it the direct way. At the Ukrainian booth, a grandmother in an embroidered shirt was handing out perogies, so he asked her what she would write on the census for origin. "Ukrainian and Scottish," she said. "My mother's family came from near Kyiv, my father's from Glasgow." At the next table a girl about his age, Priya, was taping up a banner that said Trinidad AND Portugal, and she laughed when he raised his eyebrows. "My dad's side is Indo-Trinidadian, my mom's Portuguese. It's all me." Sawyer wrote both answers down. Three booths later, a man selling bannock told him, "Cree and Irish, on my mother's side and my father's," and pointed at his own display, which showed two family trees side by side.

Sawyer sat back down and tried to clarify the pattern in his notes. Nobody had picked just one origin except a few people, and that was what he needed to check. He walked the booths for another hour, asking his question at every table, and the answers stayed consistent: most people gave him two, some gave him three. That was the hidden cause. The census numbers were not counting people. They were counting origins, and the same person could be in more than one bar on his graph.

When he got home he searched the census pages until he found the sentence, and it matched exactly what the booths had shown him. People had been able to report more than one ethnic or cultural origin since 1981, which meant the origin totals added up to more than the whole population of Canada. His graph was not broken. His arithmetic was fine. The bars were simply overlapping, the way Priya's banner overlapped two countries.

The next morning at the festival, Sawyer added a strip of paper above his bars: One person can be in more than one bar. That's not a mistake. He watched a man stop, read it, and trace the Scottish and Cree bars with one finger, nodding slowly. "My kids are all three of these," the man said, tapping Ukrainian too. "Draw me in there twice."

activity: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
knowledge_domain: to spot foreshadowing and symbolism in a short story and explain what they suggest
fact: A red herring is a false clue placed on purpose to lead readers toward the wrong conclusion, so not every hint in a story is real foreshadowing.
story:
The Tuesday book club met in the library's back corner, between the biography shelves and a radiator that clanked like it had opinions. Mila had read "The Lighthouse Keeper's Daughter" twice, once diligently with a pencil and once in a blanket fort, and she came to the meeting with a theory she was almost proud of. On page twelve, the keeper's lantern had a crack in the glass. On page forty, a ship vanished. Everyone at the table knew what that meant. The keeper had let the light fail. He was guilty.

"Obviously he did it," said Devon, who had read only the back cover. "The cracked lantern is foreshadowing. It's practically a confession."

Mila wanted to agree. The crack was the kind of detail teachers circled in red pen. But something bothered her, the way a pebble in a shoe bothers you only when you stop walking. The crack was mentioned once and then never again. The keeper repaired it on page thirteen, cheerfully, humming. Real foreshadowing, she thought, should lean forward, pointing at something ahead, not sit there like a forgotten sandwich. So she tried an experiment. She wrote the clue on an index card, flipped it over, and wrote on the back: what if this is here to make me look the wrong way?

The librarian, Ms. Okoye, wheeled past with a cart of returns and paused long enough to hear Devon declare the keeper guilty beyond doubt. "You should finish chapter nine before you vote," she said, and kept rolling, which was the most anyone at that library ever interfered with anything.

They read chapter nine. The ship had not vanished at all; it had detoured around a storm and docked two towns over, and the keeper's log proved his light burned all night. The crack on page twelve had done exactly nothing. Devon stared at his copy like it had lied to him personally. "Then why was it in there?"

"To fool you," Mila said. "It's a red herring. A false clue, put in on purpose so readers leap to the wrong conclusion." She held up her index card, front and back. "Not every hint is real foreshadowing. Some of them are traps."

Devon argued for a while, then ceased, because Ms. Okoye had returned and was standing there with the sequel, which she placed gently in front of him. On its cover, a herring, bright red, and a lighthouse with glass so clean it could have passed a hygiene inspection.

"The new one has a clue about a leaking boat," Devon said warily.

Mila sharpened her pencil. "Then we'd better decide if that boat leaks on purpose."

activity: going on a family trip away from home
knowledge_domain: going on a family trip away from home
fact: Fire-safety guidance says to put out a campfire by drowning it with water, stirring the ashes, and drowning it again until everything is cool to the touch.
story:
Alexis sat on the end of the hotel bed with one sneaker on and one in her hand, listening to the rain hammer the window. When the storm rolled in that afternoon, Dad had bailed on the campsite in a rush, dragging everyone and half the gear into the van, and now they were thirty minutes away in a room that smelled like carpet cleaner. Her little brother Theo was trying to see if he could fit entirely inside the hotel ice bucket, which he could not.

"Dad," Alexis said. "The fire pit. It was still warm when we left. I put my hand over it before we got in the van."

"It's pouring," Dad said from behind his phone. "Nothing's surviving that."

But Alexis kept thinking. Rain falls on the top of a fire pit, and the top is ash, and ash is like a blanket. Under the blanket, something could stay hot and dry while everything above it soaked. She couldn't see under there, which was exactly the problem. She thought about how the coals had looked last night, how the orange had gone gray but lumpy, like the heat was hiding rather than gone.

"Rain covers the ash," she said. "It doesn't necessarily get underneath it. Remember when it rained at home and the inside of the woodpile stayed dry?" Theo's head popped out of the ice bucket. "Are you saying the fire is a secret agent?" he asked. "Yes," Alexis said. "A secret agent of arson." Dad sighed the sigh of a man still paying the mortgage on a house he did not want to burn down along with half a state park, and reached for the van keys.

At the campsite the rain had thinned to a drizzle, and the woods around them looked lush and steaming, every leaf shiny. The fire pit was a black, soggy lump. Alexis fetched the big water jug from the van and poured the whole thing over the pit until water overflowed the stone rim. Then she grabbed a stick and stirred the drowned ashes, digging down through the layers, and a hiss rose up and a curl of steam escaped from the middle, exactly where she had guessed the blanket had been doing its job. "Ha," she said. "There you are."

She stirred until the whole pit was a cold, gray soup, then poured a second jug of water over it, because once felt like not enough. Then she did what she'd been planning the whole drive over. She pulled back her sleeve and pressed her palm flat against the ashes, holding it there. The mix was soggy and gritty and completely cool to the touch, no warmth anywhere, not even down deep where she pushed her fingers in. Theo did the same on his side and made a face. "It's like cold oatmeal," he said. "Cold oatmeal that used to be a criminal."

Back at the hotel, they came through the door dripping, and Dad went straight for the free cookies on the front desk while Mom handed out towels. "So tomorrow," Mom said, "we drive home with no secret agents?" "None," Alexis said. Theo held up his palm, still gray with ash, and said, "I kept the evidence."
